title: Digital signatures in code
summary: Sign with ECDSA and RSA-PSS, verify with only the public key, and know exactly when a MAC is the better tool.

steps.title: Sign with private, verify with public
body: The *Certificates & PKI* topic explains what a valid signature proves (integrity, and possession of the private key) and what it does not (who owns the key). Here is the code.
```csharp
using var signer = ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256);
byte[] sig = signer.SignData(data, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);            // 64 bytes
bool ok = verifier.VerifyData(data, sig, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);     // public key only

`SignData` hashes the data and signs the hash. **ECDSA and RSA-PSS signatures are randomized**: signing the same data twice gives two different signatures, and both verify. So you never compare signatures with each other; you *verify* them.

ECDSA's randomness is critical: if the per-signature random number `k` ever repeats, the private key falls out with simple algebra. Sony's PlayStation 3 used a constant `k` in 2010 and lost its master signing key. .NET generates `k` correctly for you.

steps.explain: A P-256 signature is two 32-byte numbers (r, s). Two signatures of the same data differ, yet both verify. Comparing signatures for equality would wrongly reject the second.

steps.title: MAC or signature?
body: | | HMAC | Signature (ECDSA, RSA-PSS) |
| Keys | one shared secret | private signs, public verifies |
| Who can verify | only key holders | anyone with the public key |
| Who can forge | **every** verifier (they hold the same key) | only the private-key holder |
| Non-repudiation | no | yes |
| Speed | very fast | slower (ECDSA ~ thousands/s; RSA verify fast, sign slow) |
| Size | 32 bytes | 64 (P-256) or 256 (RSA-2048) bytes |

Rule of thumb: if the signer and every verifier are **you** (your servers, your cookies, your internal tokens), an HMAC is simpler and faster. If verifiers are **other people** who must not be able to forge (software updates, public APIs, JWTs consumed by third parties, documents), use a signature.

items: Your own server signs and later checks its session cookies
A vendor signs installers that millions of users verify
An identity provider issues JWTs that many unrelated APIs validate
Two internal services that share a key authenticate requests
A bank needs proof a customer approved a transfer
A webhook provider and one customer share a secret per endpoint
steps.explain: Ask who verifies and whether a verifier could be tempted to forge. Shared keys mean every verifier is also a potential forger.

steps.title: RSA signature paddings
body: RSA signs too, with its own paddings:
- **PSS** (`RSASignaturePadding.Pss`): randomized, with a security proof. Prefer it for new designs (`PS256` in JWT).

- **PKCS#1 v1.5** (`RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1`): deterministic, still considered secure for *signatures* and used everywhere (`RS256` in JWT, most certificates). Unlike v1.5 *encryption*, it has no practical attack when verified properly.
```csharp
byte[] sig = rsa.SignData(data, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pss);
bool ok = rsa.VerifyData(data, sig, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pss);
The *Authentication & JWT* topic's lesson **RS256 and ES256** uses exactly these calls to sign tokens.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `True False`.
code: byte[] doc = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("I owe Bob 10 EUR");
bool ok = rsa.__2__(doc, sig, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.__3__);
bool forged = rsa.__2__(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("I owe Bob 1000 EUR"), sig, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.__3__);
steps.explain: `SignData` and `VerifyData` hash for you. A changed amount gives a different hash, so verification fails.

steps.prompt: A developer verifies an ECDSA signature by re-signing the received data with the public key and comparing the two signatures. What is wrong?
options: Everything: you cannot sign with a public key, and ECDSA signatures differ every time anyway; call VerifyData
Nothing, it is a valid shortcut
It works for RSA-PSS but not ECDSA
It only needs a constant-time comparison
steps.explain: Verification is its own operation. Signing needs the private key, and randomized signatures never match byte for byte.

steps.title: Sign and verify a release
prompt: - `byte[] SignRelease(ECDsa key, string manifest)`: ECDSA over the UTF-8 bytes with SHA-256.
- `bool VerifyRelease(byte[] publicKey, string manifest, byte[] signature)`: import `publicKey` (SubjectPublicKeyInfo bytes) into a fresh `ECDsa` and verify. The verifier never sees the private key.
The tests check a good signature, an edited manifest, a signature from the wrong key, and a damaged signature.
starter: bool VerifyRelease(byte[] publicKey, string manifest, byte[] signature)
solution: bool VerifyRelease(byte[] publicKey, string manifest, byte[] signature)
template: Dojo.Eq("a P-256 signature is 64 bytes", 64, dojoSig.Length);
Dojo.Check("the vendor's signature verifies", VerifyRelease(dojoPub, dojoManifest, dojoSig), "VerifyRelease rejected a good signature");
Dojo.Check("an edited manifest fails", !VerifyRelease(dojoPub, dojoManifest.Replace("1.4.2", "1.4.3"), dojoSig), "accepted an edited manifest");
Dojo.Check("Mallory's signature fails", !VerifyRelease(dojoPub, dojoManifest, SignRelease(dojoMallory, dojoManifest)), "accepted a signature from another key");
Dojo.Check("a damaged signature fails", !VerifyRelease(dojoPub, dojoManifest, dojoBad), "accepted a damaged signature");

steps.title: Sign a contract with RSA-PSS
prompt: Write a program that creates one RSA-2048 key, signs the contract text `"Alice sells Bob 1 bike for 100 EUR"` with **PSS** and SHA-256, and prints exactly:
- *altered*: verify the same signature against `"Alice sells Bob 1 bike for 10 EUR"`.
- *repeat*: sign the original again and compare the two signatures byte for byte.
- *wrong padding*: verify the original PSS signature with `RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1` (padding is part of the algorithm).
starter: byte[] contract = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("Alice sells Bob 1 bike for 100 EUR");
solution: byte[] contract = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("Alice sells Bob 1 bike for 100 EUR");
byte[] altered = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("Alice sells Bob 1 bike for 10 EUR");
Console.WriteLine($"wrong padding verifies: {rsa.VerifyData(contract, sig, sha, RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1)}");
hints: `VerifyData` returns `false` (it does not throw) for a bad signature.
